title: When a neighbor's cup breaks
hook: when someone else's cup breaks we say "these things happen," so say it of your own (Enchiridion 26)

segments.voice: Yesterday: the price of lettuce, the obol that buys it. Your line was I kept the coin. Did you notice a price you didn't pay, and what you kept? Day three hundred fifty-eight.

A friend texts: I dented my car backing out of the garage. Your reply takes four seconds. Oh no! Happens to everyone. Is anyone hurt? That's what matters. Wise, calm, kind. A week later you dent your own car backing out of your own garage, and for the next hour you're a different person. Idiot. How could I. This always happens to me. Same kind of dent. Same kind of morning. Somehow you had perfect perspective for your friend and none at all for yourself. Section twenty-six of the handbook says the wisdom you need was in that four-second text. Today: when a neighbor's cup breaks.
screen: `A FRIEND'S DENTED CAR.` → `HAPPENS TO EVERYONE.` → `THEN IT'S YOUR CAR.`

segments.voice: First, the method. What nature intends, Epictetus says, we can learn from the cases where we all agree. Not from arguments. From our own easy answers about other people's troubles. Second, the cup. When someone else's servant breaks a cup, we're quick to say: these things happen. So, he says, when your own cup breaks, be the same as you were when the other one broke. That's all. Borrow your own good advice. Third, bigger things. Then he carries it further, gently but firmly. When someone else's child or spouse dies, everyone says: that's the human lot. But when it's one's own, right away it's: oh, poor me, how wretched. We ought to remember, he says, how we felt when we heard the same news about others. Here it's worth slowing down, because this is a hard line to hear. Epictetus asks a great deal: the same steadiness for your own loss as for a stranger's. Not every reader will follow him that far, and nobody here is asked to. But the part anyone can use is narrower. It's the doubled suffering, the sense that this, unlike everyone else's, shouldn't have happened, that the world has made an exception of you. Fourth, the practice under it. Often the wise, steady friend who knows exactly what to say about broken cups is already in the room. It's us, talking to someone else. The trick is to turn around and say it to ourselves, with the same warmth. It's strangely close to the old rule about loving your neighbor as yourself, only running backward. Treat yourself, for a moment, as you'd treat your neighbor. These things happen. To them. To you.
screen: `LEARN FROM WHERE WE AGREE.` · `ANOTHER'S CUP: THESE THINGS HAPPEN.` · `THE HARDER CASE.` · `SAY IT TO YOURSELF, WARMLY.` · then, large: `THESE THINGS HAPPEN.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one trouble of your own that's been weighing on you. Something manageable: a mistake, a breakage, a bad week. Now imagine a friend telling you that exact story, as if it happened to them. Listen to them. What would you say? Let the words come, kind and steady. Then turn them around and say them to yourself, in the same tone. These things happen. Stay with that. The bell holds the time.
Cup. When a neighbor's breaks, Epictetus says, we're quick with calm and good advice; turn that same wisdom on your own. Today's word.
Your line: these things happen. When something of yours breaks today, say what you'd say to a friend, and mean it for yourself. Day three hundred fifty-eight.

howItsDone: Some Stoic practitioners treat their own setbacks the way they would a friend's, using the same calm words they would readily offer someone else.

notes: Review (2026-10-01): SERIOUS fix: the teach said 'Epictetus isn't saying grief is wrong', which misstates Stoic teaching (Ench 26 asks for the same calm at one's own loss); it now says plainly that he asks a great deal and the listener isn't asked to follow. Replaced the matching myth; cut 'readers have long found', 'most of us' and the uncited trapdoor claim; fixed 'same garage' (it was the listener's own).

Enchiridion 26 paraphrased (the will of nature learned from things in which we don't differ; another's slave breaks a cup; another's child or wife dies, 'it is the lot of man'; one's own, 'alas, how wretched I am'). Confirm.
'the old rule about loving your neighbor as yourself' alluded to (Leviticus 19:18; Matthew 22:39) without quotation; a neighbor mention, not a comparison.
Sensitive: deaths of a child or spouse named once, with an explicit note that grief isn't called wrong.
Distinct from day 335 (jug): this day is about transferring one's calm for others to oneself.
